newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia diamond seizure one more blow for De Beers.
newsitem.headline: Russia diamond seizure one more blow for De Beers.

text.p: A possibly lengthy reevaluation of Russian gems owned by South African diamond giant De Beers threatens to further tarnish what has already been a difficult year for the firm in Russia's evolving diamond sector.
Gems worth around $200 million, which were seized by customs officials last month, have been handed over to Gokhran, Russia's state strategic reserve and part of the Finance Ministry.
Gokhran said the diamonds had been undervalued by Russia's diamond monopoly, Almazy Rossii-Sakha (ARS), and is insisting on reassessing their price.
"The diamonds are with Gokhran, where they are undergoing what is called 'expertise'," said Raymond Clarke, head of De Beers' Moscow representation.
A spokesman for ARS said the re-evaluation process could take several weeks to complete, but he hoped the issue would be resolved in July.
De Beers owns around $150 million of the batch, the remainder belonging to other companies including ARS, ARS said.
The sums involved are unlikely to bring either company to ruin, but the repercussions of the seizure on Russia's gem business could go much further than the hold-up itself.

ARS linked the gem seizure to a battle for control of the lucrative gem export market, previously dominated by trade agreements between ARS and De Beers. But the spokesman refrained from blaming any particular parties.

"Yes, the confiscation of these goods is connected with an internal struggle for control of Russia's diamond export business," he said. But he said Gokhran and ARS had reached an "understanding" on the problem.
He also said it could delay further the signing of a gem trade deal between ARS and De Beers.
The last agreement expired at the end of 1996, and Moscow has failed to give the final seal of approval to a draft deal submitted to the cabinet way back in October last year.
"If the government wants to sort out this problem first, then yes, there could be a physical reason for further delays in the deal," the ARS spokesman said.
He did not fully rule out the possibility that the row over the diamonds' value could break the deal altogether, but added ARS still expected an agreement to be signed.
"This would be the extreme, and of course extremes exist. But we still think there will be a deal -- the company and Russian people still want De Beers to continue to work here."

De Beers' Clarke said he would make no direct link between the seizure of the diamonds and the delays in signing the agreement. But on Tuesday he did say it was "fair" to look at the possibility of there being no gem deal with ARS.
"I think it is fair to ask that question, given the delays," he said then. "My answer is that we will cooperate with Russia either informally or formally. Life won't come to an end (without a deal)."
De Beers has already announced it is interested in a stake in the huge Lomonosov diamond deposit, containing an estimated $12 billion worth of gems.
ARS said the misunderstanding between it and Gokhran was caused by differing methods, and nothing more sinister.
ARS based its valuation on world prices, which were lower than domestic prices, the basis for Gokhran's evaluation, the spokesman said.
"This is a question of methodology connected with problems of giving a correct assessment of the price of the parcels."

The diamonds were sent to the airport before the end of May to qualify for a special "export window" allowing exports from Russia until the end of May. The government has not issued a decree outlining export quota allowances for the rest of 1997.
De Beers said they were confident the diamonds could be exported once the assessment was completed, even though the end-May deadline has passed.
"We have been led to believe that the goods will leave the country eventually under that quota," Clarke said.

De Beers and ARS have been frustrated repeatedly by senior government officials promising a swift end to delays both to the trade deal and export quota decree, but so far they have failed to deliver the goods.
Russia accounted for 26 percent of De Beers' total worldwide sales under the previous gem trade deal, which was worth around $1.2 billion a year to Russia.
